newsitem.title: UK: RUGBY UNION-FIVE MINUTES OF MAYHEM ROCK SCOTLAND.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-FIVE MINUTES OF MAYHEM ROCK SCOTLAND.

text.p: Five minutes of Murrayfield mayhem signalled Wales' continued rugby renaissance on an opening day of the Five Nations championship which saw victories for both visiting teams on Saturday.

A burst of three tries inside five second half minutes led Wales to a thumping 34-19 triumph over a shell-shocked Scotland while France opened their campaign with a more expected 32-15 win against Ireland in Dublin.
French flair deservedly won the day at Lansdowne Road after five penalties from recalled fly-half Eric Elwood had briefly put a dogged Ireland 15-12 in the lead.
But then in stepped left-wing David Venditti to complete a hat-trick of tries as holes appeared in Ireland's defence. The more the Irish attempted to attack, the more in control the French became.
Newly-appointed coach Brian Ashton admitted his side had capitulated in the latter stages.
"For 60 minutes we competed remarkably well. Unfortunately test rugby matches last 80 minutes and in the last 20 we lost our shape," he said.

Not that French coach Jean-Claude Skrela was entirely happy either, saying his team had given the ball away too often and adding they had a lot of work to do ahead of the remaining Five Nations matches.
Ireland have not beaten France in Dublin since 1983, somewhat surprisingly exactly the same length of time since they last lost to Wales in Cardiff where they play their next Five Nations fixture.
That record may be difficult to keep intact on the evidence of Wales' second half performance against Scotland.
Scotland had turned round 13-10 ahead and quickly added a further three points before a nightmare five minutes shattered their hopes and their confidence.

Full-back Neil Jenkins, who became only the fifth player to amass more than 500 points in test rugby, cut in from the left to touch down; fly-half Arwel Thomas made the most of a fortunate bounce to score a runaway try and winger Ieuan Evans won the chase for a kick ahead to add another.
Scottish manager Arthur Hastie called it a "fatal five minutes" while captain Rob Wainwright said it was a lack of concentration which cost them the game.
"We've got to blame ourselves. They were real punches in the eye. Letting yourself down in that manner is unforgiveable," Wainwright said.
Bookmakers still make England, who did not play in the opening round of matches, favourites to win the championship.
